cards.b: A black hole is a region where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape. It is the logical end of Einstein's general relativity, and the best place to test it. It also anchors the centre of most big galaxies and powers the brightest objects in the universe.

cards.h: An old idea, a new theory
cards.b: In 1783 John Michell, and later Laplace, wondered: if a star were massive enough, its escape speed would exceed the speed of light and it would be dark. Einstein's general relativity (1915) turned this into a theory. In 1916 Karl Schwarzschild found the exact solution, giving a radius at which escape is impossible.

The Schwarzschild radius is r = 2GM/c squared. For the Sun it is about 3 km; for Earth about 9 mm. If the Sun were squeezed into a ball of 3 km, it would be a black hole. The surface at that radius is the event horizon: a one-way door. Cross it and no signal can return.

At the centre, general relativity predicts a singularity, where density and curvature become infinite, a sign that the theory breaks down and quantum gravity is needed. Near a stellar-mass black hole, tides stretch you like spaghetti. Distant observers see a falling clock slow down and fade at the horizon, though the faller notices nothing special when crossing a large horizon.

• Stellar-mass (a few to tens of Suns): from collapsing massive stars.
  • Supermassive (millions to billions of Suns): in galaxy centres. Our Milky Way's Sagittarius A* has about 4 million Suns; M87's about 6.5 billion.
  • Intermediate: a few thousand Suns, now being found.

How supermassive ones grew so large so early is a live question.

A black hole emits no light, but matter spiralling in forms a hot accretion disc that glows in X-rays, and jets can blaze across a galaxy. Cygnus X-1 (1971) was the first strong candidate. Stars orbiting the Milky Way's centre revealed Sgr A*; this won the 2020 Nobel Prize (Genzel and Ghez), shared with Roger Penrose for proving that black holes follow from relativity (1965).

In 1974 Stephen Hawking showed that quantum effects near the horizon make black holes emit a faint glow and slowly lose mass. For a stellar-mass hole it is far too small to detect and the lifetime is vastly longer than the universe's age. It links gravity, quantum theory and thermodynamics.

In 2015 LIGO heard two black holes merge. In April 2019 the Event Horizon Telescope released the first image of a black hole shadow, M87*, and in May 2022 one of Sgr A*, in our own galaxy. Both matched Einstein's predictions.

• 'Black holes suck in everything.' If the Sun became a black hole of equal mass, Earth would keep orbiting normally.
  • 'They are holes.' They are objects with mass.
  • 'Nobody has seen one.' We have images and gravitational-wave detections.

The Chandrasekhar limit (1930) showed that heavy enough stars cannot stop collapsing: the first step to black holes. Amal Kumar Raychaudhuri derived in 1955 the Raychaudhuri equation, a key ingredient in the Penrose-Hawking singularity theorems. ISRO's AstroSat found in 2017 rapid X-ray pulsations in the black hole system GRS 1915+105 and studied Cygnus X-1.

• A black hole is a region of no escape, bounded by an event horizon of radius 2GM/c squared.
  • Stellar ones come from massive stars; supermassive ones sit in galaxy centres.
  • We detect them by accretion light, orbiting stars, gravitational waves and shadow images.
  • Hawking radiation hints at a link with quantum physics.

Think about it: (1) Why would the Sun, as a black hole, not change Earth's orbit? (2) Why is the singularity a sign of incomplete physics?

o: Boundary beyond which nothing can escape
